title.narrative: Sawasya III Rule of Law Palestine
Sawasya III Rättsstatens Principer i Palestina

description.narrative: Sawasya III is a comprehensive United Nations joint programme that aims to advance the promotion, respect for, and fulfilment of human rights and gender equality across the occupied Palestinian. It is jointly implemented by UNDP, UN Women, and UNICEF and supported by a donor consortium. Sawasya III centres around people’s needs for providing higher quality services within more responsive institutions and fostering inclusiveness, while addressing resistance to change. The aim is to reinforce equal justice for all, with a particular emphasis on the most at-risk groups, which serves as a critical measure of progress towards a cohesive, democratic, and inclusive society that respects human rights. Sawasya III adopts a people-centred justice approach in line with the UN's global approach to RoL programs and Sidas poor people’s perspective and rights based approach. Five Palestinian justice sector agencies sign the program document: the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Social Development, the High Judicial Council, the Attorney General’s office and the Sharia Courts. The program also relies on effective alliances with Palestinian CSO, who support the program in various areas including awareness raising, legal aid, court monitoring, and advocacy.

Sawasya III är ett omfattande FN program som syftar till att främja respekten för och uppfyllandet av mänskliga rättigheter och jämställdhet i Palestina. Det genomförs gemensamt av UNDP, UN Women och UNICEF och stöds av ett givarkonsortium. Sawasya III fokuserar på människors behov av service av god kvalité vilken ska tillhandahållas av institutioner med kapacitet att vara lyhörda och främja inkludering. Sawasya arbetar även med att minska motstånd mot nödvändig förändring. Syftet är att främja lika rättvisa för alla, med särskild tonvikt på de mest utsatta grupperna. Något som även är en måttstock på framsteg mot ett sammanhållet, demokratiskt och inkluderande samhälle som respekterar mänskliga rättigheter. Fokus ligger alltså på rättighetsbärarnas perspektiv i linje med FN:s globala syn på RoL-program och Sida’s fattigdomsperspektiv och rättighetsbaserade ansats. Fem palestinska myndigheter inom rättssektorn undertecknar programdokumentet; justitieministeriet, ministeriet för social utveckling, det höga rättsliga rådet, riksåklagarens kontor och shariadomstolarna. Programmet förlitar sig också på effektiva allianser med palestinska CSO, som stöder programmet inom olika områden, inklusive medvetenhetshöjande, rättshjälp, domstolsövervakning och påverkansarbete.

The over all goal of Swasya is: People in the State of Palestine, especially women and children, have access to justice in a protective, inclusive and responsive system that promotes, respects, and fulfils human rights and gender equality.
There are four programme outcomes listed under this goal:
Outcome 1: People, particularly those at risk, have improved access to high-quality services relating to their legal, psychosocial, protection, and security needs
Outcome 2: People are served by responsive institutions that have strengthened capacity to operate in an effective, efficient, peoplecentred, and accountable manner
Outcome 3: Societal and institutional behaviours and attitudes that uphold human rights, gender equality, and equity principles are embraced.
Outcome 4: Womens access to gender responsive and inclusive justice, security and protection services is strengthened..

Despite the political context Sawasya finds it possible to implement its work plan, with tangible results. Among them are the establishment of specialized services for women victims and survivors of violence, the enhancement of child justice frameworks and the recognition of digital justice innovations. A narrative report was submitted to Sida in May 2025 accounting for results during 2024, which was the first year for Sawasya III. When assessing Sawasya's results there are both long term results as well as immediate results for beneficiaries. One example is the implementation of the digital system Mizan. In a long term perspective it will increase the robustness of the judicial system and make it more accessible to both professionals and end users. In a short term perspective it gives immediate results for individuals who use it. 30 civil society organisations have been contracted to expand services in legal representation, consultation, legal awareness and psychosocial services, benefiting women and children directly. Another example of more long term results is the work on legislative, legal and policy framework like the Family Protection Bill and Family Laws. In 2024, a total of 15 legal instruments were amended or introduced to align with gender justice and human rights standards. A concrete example of how Sawasya has supported people with disabilities is the development of a Legal Sign Dictionary. It was developed by the Palestinian Union for the Deaf and the High Judicial Council, with support from Sawasya. The dictionary simplifies legal processes and ensures that people with hearing disabilities can access their rights and prevent misunderstandings. In strengthening children's justice Sawasya supported the development of comprehensive judicial guidelines and a toolkit aligned with international human rights standards, which enhance the wellbeing of children in care or detention. Three judges received specialized training in Amman, equipping them with essential knowledge on inspecting custodial and noncustodial settings. The program also provided specialized diplomas to 47 front line personnel enhancing capacity to safeguard children's rights. Police officers have been trained on conducting child friendly interviews. In 2024, approximately 2,500 children in the West Bank came into contact with the law, with a 50 percent increase in the involvement of girls, compared to previous year. Both boys and girls faced charges related to harm, underscoring the ongoing cycle of violence fueled by unstable environment. The Sawasya program has expanded its child protection services, providing comprehensive legal aid, mental health and psychosocial support, case management and legal counselling. The program also focused on the rehabilitation and reintegration of children in conflict with the law, by implementing initiatives like therapeutic activities, life skills program and vocational training.
Improving women's access to justice Sawasya has supported institutions to review and amend the Violence Against Women Specialized services in line with the National Referral System, which includes components related to women with disabilities. Supporting the Chief Justice decision in approving the institutionalization of services for "violence against women" in courts, will ensure that women's cases in courts are only managed by specialized judges. Advocacy efforts have contributed to increased female representation in the justice sector the proportion of female judges has risen by over 5 percent, prosecutors by 7 percent and police officers from 4 percent to 6.8 percent in 2024. During 2024 the program continued to provide critical support for specific cases of violence against women, contributing to strengthened access to justice for survivors. Integrated legal aid, legal awareness and psychosocial services are important to empower women to take legal action against perpetrators of violence. Critical support is given through "One Stop Centres" which aim to enhance coordination, improve service delivery and ensure a gender responsive justice system. They offer a holistic environment for survivors to seek medical and legal support within a safe, where specialized professionals from various sectors come together under one roof. In 2024 the digital Mizan court management system was advanced, digitizing case management and court procedure to address movement restrictions impacting access to justice. The system enabled remote access to judicial processes, ensuring continuity of operations for judges and prosecutors despite mobility constraints. The impact of Mizan was manifested by a second place among more than 1,100 global submissions, in the 2024 SDG Digital Game Changers Award. Its scalability, replicability and focus on vulnerable populations, particularly women and children, were important factors in this recognition. Sawasya enhanced the quality of legal education through strategic partnership with three leading law schools AlQuds, AnNajah and Birzeit University.
The annual report gives a range of specific numbers on how people have benefited from the program Legal aid 13,517 Palestinians of which 11,182 women accessed legal aid, consultation and representation 21,054 Palestinians of which 16,433 women received legal awareness Children's access to justice and psychosocial support, 1,164 juvenile cases benefited from mediation services 396 children received legal counselling, 268 children received individual and structured psychosocial support 204 children benefited from reintegration and rehabilitation programs, 1,700 cases on Violence against Women were referred from the public prosecutor to the courts. Ultimately, 456 cases resulted in a conviction 653 women benefited from the services of One Stop Centres in Ramallah, Nablus and Hebron 10,969 women survivors of violence referred to specialized services within the national referral system .Capacity development for justice and social justice providers 353 justice and social justice providers, including 215 women, benefited from specialized capacity development and 330 justice and social justice providers received training through certified programmes
380 students, graduates and practitioners, including 229 women, benefited from legal programs, including clinical training. 164,661 individuals of the general public accessed the digital case management system Mizan. Among the users were also 272 judges, 169 public prosecutors, 7,877 lawyers and 2,569 court staff member. Approximately 86,200 documents related to case management were archived.
